primary_cause: Market pricing of an imminent spike in credit losses and a severe hit to travel-related card spending. No discrete AXP headline in the prior 3 days but AXP was highly exposed to the travel-and-entertainment collapse
secondary_factors: April 1 macro deterioration in jobs/manufacturing and broad selloff in financials
store_description: AXP was one of the most travel-sensitive card issuers so the market likely looked through to a very weak Q1 and worse Q2 as airline hotel and entertainment spend vanished. Later-reported provisions surged to $2.6 billion and profit fell roughly 76% which validates why AXP fell harder than many non-financials on April 1.

primary_cause: Semiconductor-sector de-risking on worsening global demand assumptions rather than an AMD-specific event. No meaningful AMD-specific headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: April 1 manufacturing contraction and broad Nasdaq weakness
store_description: AMD's decline looks like a sector read-through from collapsing consumer electronics expectations rather than company-specific bad news. With 2020 iPhone shipment forecasts already being cut from 204 million to 198 million investors were repricing chip demand broadly across PCs handsets and consumer hardware.

primary_cause: No clear stock-specific catalyst found. Likely valuation compression in software and digital-media names as the economic outlook worsened
secondary_factors: April 1 macro shock and risk-off in tech with concerns over enterprise spending freezes
store_description: Adobe had already reported earnings in mid-March so the April 1 move does not appear tied to a new company disclosure. The most plausible explanation is broad multiple compression in high-quality software names as investors shifted from remote work winners to recession math.

primary_cause: Recession fears hitting IT services and consulting budgets. No fresh Accenture-specific headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Broad selloff in cyclically exposed enterprise-services names on worsening macro data
store_description: Accenture's business is highly sensitive to delayed client projects and discretionary consulting spend. With U.S. manufacturing contracting and labor-market expectations deteriorating rapidly the market likely sold ACN as a high-quality cyclical rather than on any one company headline.

primary_cause: Defensive healthcare still getting dragged lower by the broad market not a clear company-specific shock. No negative AbbVie-specific March 29 to April 1 headline
secondary_factors: Merger-execution uncertainty around Allergan and general COVID-driven de-risking
store_description: ABBV held up better than most of the list which fits the absence of a strong negative company-specific catalyst. The stock was probably pressured mainly by broad risk-off conditions with some residual uncertainty around the large Allergan transaction.

primary_cause: Weakening iPhone demand expectations from COVID. Reuters reported on March 27 that suppliers were worried about demand with one research shop cutting Q1 iPhone shipments to 35 million from 41 million and 2020 shipments to 198 million from 204 million
secondary_factors: Ongoing retail disruption outside China and broad tech selloff
store_description: Apple's April 1 drop looks strongly tied to the demand side of COVID not only supply-chain noise. By March 27 the key incremental signal was that production was recovering but end demand was deteriorating with projected 2020 iPhone shipments cut by about 6 million units.

primary_cause: Recession fears for enterprise hardware services and legacy IT spending. No meaningful IBM-specific headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Broad April 1 tech and cyclical selloff with no offsetting positive IBM catalyst
store_description: IBM's move looks macro- and sector-driven with investors discounting delayed enterprise projects weaker consulting demand and pressure on infrastructure spending which fit IBM's profile even without a fresh company headline.

primary_cause: REIT and rate-sensitive equity selling during a broad liquidity-driven risk-off move. No company-specific negative AMT headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Generalized pressure on real estate securities despite towers being relatively defensive
store_description: AMT's fall appears more like indiscriminate REIT selling than tower-specific fundamental deterioration. The size of the move was notable given tower assets were more resilient than retail or hotel real estate suggesting the stock was caught in portfolio-level liquidation.

primary_cause: NBCUniversal/theme-park and movie-business damage from the pandemic. Reuters reported on March 24 that Comcast said COVID would materially impact results and operations delay film distribution and force theme-park closures
secondary_factors: Ad-market fears and general media-sector weakness with brand advertising weakening materially in mid-March
store_description: Comcast was not just a cable broadband story on April 1. Investors were likely focusing on the sudden evaporation of high-margin theme-park and film revenue after management said COVID would materially hurt operations while the broader advertising market was also deteriorating quickly.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and hardware demand fears especially tied to smartphones and enterprise hardware. No fresh Broadcom-specific headline in the prior 3 days
secondary_factors: Apple demand concerns and broad chip-sector derating
store_description: Broadcom traded down more like a cyclical semiconductor name than a software or defensive tech name. With Apple unit expectations being revised lower and global manufacturing contracting investors were likely pricing weaker wireless enterprise and industrial chip demand into AVGO.

primary_cause: Collapsing crude demand and oil-price expectations. Reuters reported on March 31 that oil had just posted its biggest monthly and quarterly losses ever with major forecasters expecting 20% to 30% demand destruction in April
secondary_factors: Residual shock from the Saudi-Russia price war and recession fears
store_description: COP fell less than some other cyclicals because oil had already been crushed but the driver was still clearly commodity-linked. The market was looking at an unprecedented collapse in fuel demand and an oil market that had just completed its worst month and quarter on record.

primary_cause: Extreme concern about consumer credit deterioration especially subprime-ish card and auto exposure. Capital One later reported a Q1 net loss of $1.3 billion with about $5 billion of loss reserves
secondary_factors: Financial-sector selloff and worsening labor outlook
store_description: COF's drop was much steeper than AXP's because the market saw it as more exposed to unemployment-driven charge-offs and stressed households. The later numbers support that view with a $1.3 billion quarterly loss and about $5 billion of reserves.

primary_cause: Financial-system stress and recession repricing. Reuters reported Goldman said on March 23 that global GDP would contract about 1% in 2020 and noted intense stress in money markets with Goldman pouring more than $1 billion into prime money-market portfolios
secondary_factors: Broad pressure on banks and broker-dealers from April 1 macro data
store_description: GS was being traded as both a bank and a market-plumbing institution during a period of extraordinary funding stress. The combination of Goldman's own recession call and evidence of money-market strain likely reinforced concern about trading underwriting and balance-sheet risk.

primary_cause: Ad-market collapse fears tied to small business shutdowns. By late March analysts were projecting tech giants could lose more than $40 billion in 2020 ad revenue with Google especially exposed to self-serve ad spend
secondary_factors: General big-tech de-risking and macro deterioration
store_description: Alphabet's drop looks mostly ad-driven. The market was starting to recognize that even a dominant digital ad platform could not escape a sudden freeze in travel local business and brand advertising which is why Google fell alongside other cyclical media-ad names despite its strong balance sheet.

primary_cause: Ad-market collapse fears tied to small business shutdowns. Same underlying business exposure as GOOGL with analysts forecasting large digital-ad revenue damage from COVID
secondary_factors: Broad Nasdaq weakness
store_description: There is no meaningful distinction in the cause between GOOG and GOOGL here. The market was discounting a sharp advertising slowdown especially from small businesses and brand advertisers which made Alphabet trade more like a cyclical media company than a pure defensive tech platform.

primary_cause: Factory shutdowns and emergency liquidity actions signaling severe cash burn. Reuters reported GM drew about $16 billion from credit lines on March 24 and suspended its 2020 outlook
secondary_factors: Recession fears for auto demand and financing
store_description: GM's April 1 decline was clearly stock-specific. A company does not draw roughly $16 billion of credit suspend guidance and shut plants across the U.S. Canada and Mexico unless management expects a severe revenue shock so the move was a rational repricing of prolonged production stoppages and collapsing vehicle demand.

primary_cause: No clear stock-specific negative catalyst found. Likely a broad-market pullback after prior biotech strength with the major remdesivir readouts coming later in April and May
secondary_factors: Investors still lacked hard remdesivir efficacy data at that moment
store_description: GILD had been one of the more obvious COVID drug-exposure names but on April 1 the decisive remdesivir data had not yet arrived. This move looks more like a market-driven fade and some profit-taking rather than a reaction to new negative company information.

primary_cause: Fear that lockdowns would crush store traffic and raise labor/operating costs. Reuters reported on March 18 that Home Depot was temporarily adjusting store hours and extending paid time off
secondary_factors: Broad consumer and housing-related recession fears
store_description: On April 1 investors still had limited visibility into the later DIY boom and instead were focused on near-term disruption with shorter hours employee-related costs and weaker big-ticket demand. HD traded as a cyclical retailer exposed to shutdown risk not yet as the eventual pandemic winner.

primary_cause: GE Aviation exposure to the collapse in global air travel and worsening cash-flow fears. Reuters reported GE warned coronavirus would hit Q1 cash flow by $300 million to $500 million and the stock hit a 28-year low after aviation job cuts
secondary_factors: Investor concern over leverage/liquidity and continued industrial recession
store_description: GE was one of the clearest stock-specific losers. The market already knew by early March that COVID would hit cash flow by up to $500 million in Q1 and by late March the aviation outlook had deteriorated so sharply that the stock was back near multi-decade lows making the April 1 selloff a continuation of very specific business damage.

primary_cause: Worsening global trade and economic expectations overwhelming any partial benefit from residential deliveries. No strong FedEx-specific March 29 to April 1 headline
secondary_factors: Recession fears and supply-chain disruptions and general transportation-sector pressure
store_description: FedEx was a bellwether for world trade so the April 1 move likely reflected macro deterioration more than a new company disclosure. With manufacturing contracting and corporate activity freezing investors were pricing a sharp decline in business-to-business shipping and freight demand.
